sub: Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
def: A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that presents itself to its users as a single coherent system; cloud computing is the utility-priced, on-demand delivery of pooled computing resources over a network, defined by NIST through five essential characteristics, three service models and four deployment models; and edge computing pushes part of that processing out to nodes physically close to where the data is produced.
exp:
Read this leaf as one line of development rather than three topics. Centralised time-sharing gave way to client-server, client-server to clusters and grids, and grids to the metered, self-service cloud; edge computing is the swing back outward once the round trip to a distant region became the binding constraint. What changes at each step is where computation sits relative to the data and who absorbs the cost of idle capacity. What does not change is the set of problems a distributed system creates the moment work spans more than one machine: partial failure, in which some components fail while the rest keep running and no participant can distinguish a crashed peer from a slow one; the need for transparency of access, location, migration, replication, concurrency and failure so that the collection still reads as one system; and the fact that latency is bounded by physics and cannot be engineered away. The eight fallacies of distributed computing, usually credited to Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun, are the standard list of assumptions that break: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology does not change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, the network is homogeneous. The CAP theorem is the same lesson stated formally: a partition will happen on a wide-area network, so partition tolerance is not a design choice, and the real choice during a partition is between serving possibly stale answers and refusing to answer.

The NIST definition in SP 800-145 is the part MPSC can lift straight into a one-mark item, so learn the lists exactly. The five essential characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. The three service models are Software as a Service, Platform as a Service and Infrastructure as a Service. The four deployment models are private, community, public and hybrid. Everything else you associate with cloud marketing is outside the definition: provider-managed disaster recovery, unlimited storage, pay-as-you-go pricing as such, virtualization as such, multi-cloud and virtual private cloud are all not on any of these three lists. Note in particular that measured service means the system meters and reports usage at some level of abstraction, which is what makes billing possible, and that resource pooling carries with it the multi-tenant model and a degree of location independence, the consumer generally knowing only the region or data centre rather than the machine.

The reference architecture is a second, separate NIST document, SP 500-292, and it defines actors, not characteristics. There are five: the cloud consumer, who uses the service; the cloud provider, who makes it available; the cloud auditor, who conducts independent assessment of security, privacy, performance and operations; the cloud broker, who manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services and negotiates relationships between consumer and provider; and the cloud carrier, who provides the connectivity and transport of cloud services between provider and consumer. The broker-versus-carrier pair is the examinable one. A broker intermediates commercially and technically and its work falls into service intermediation, which improves a given service with value-added capability, service aggregation, which combines multiple services into one integrated offering, and service arbitrage, which is aggregation in which the services combined are not fixed and the broker is free to choose among providers. A carrier moves bits: network and telecommunication transport, possibly over dedicated encrypted links provided under an SLA.

Edge computing is decided by arithmetic, so do the arithmetic. Light in fibre travels at roughly 200,000 km per second, which is about 1 ms per 200 km one way, so a site 1,000 km from the region pays about 10 ms of pure propagation on a round trip before a single queue, serialisation delay or bit of processing is counted. Given an assembly-line inspection loop that must accept or reject a part within 20 ms and a measured cloud round-trip time of 60 ms, no amount of accelerator capacity or horizontal scaling in the region helps, because the deadline is already violated by the transit alone; the only fix is to move inference onto a node inside the plant. The other three drivers are bandwidth and data gravity, where shipping every camera frame to a region costs more than processing it locally and sending results; availability, where the local loop must keep working across a WAN outage; and data residency, where regulation requires the raw data stay put. Fog computing is the intermediate tier between device and region, typically a gateway or a small on-premise cluster aggregating many edge nodes. The usual division of labour in 2026 is that models are trained centrally where the accelerators and the whole dataset live, and executed at the edge.

Exam shape: in the MCQ half this leaf is mostly list recall, either an odd-one-out on the five characteristics or four deployment models, or an actor-attribution item that hangs entirely on broker versus carrier, plus one applied item that gives you a deadline and a round-trip time and asks what edge placement actually removes. In the conventional half it is squarely essay-shaped, because explain the NIST cloud computing reference architecture with its actors, or distinguish edge, fog and cloud computing with a suitable example, are both standard ten-mark questions. Marks are lost by mixing the SP 800-145 lists into the SP 500-292 answer, and by describing edge as a cost optimisation when the defining reason is latency.
facts: The five NIST essential characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.
The four NIST deployment models are private, community, public and hybrid; multi-cloud and virtual private cloud are not NIST deployment models.
The NIST cloud computing reference architecture (SP 500-292) names five actors: cloud consumer, cloud provider, cloud auditor, cloud broker and cloud carrier.
A cloud carrier provides connectivity and transport of cloud services between provider and consumer; a cloud broker manages use, performance and delivery of services and negotiates between the two.
Cloud broker services fall into three categories: service intermediation, service aggregation and service arbitrage, arbitrage differing from aggregation in that the services combined are not fixed.

The eight fallacies of distributed computing are: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology does not change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, the network is homogeneous.
Signal propagation in fibre is roughly 200,000 km/s, about 1 ms per 200 km one way, so a 1,000 km distance costs about 10 ms of round-trip propagation before any processing.
Fog computing denotes the intermediate tier between edge devices and the cloud region, typically an on-premise gateway or small cluster aggregating many edge nodes.
Under CAP, partition tolerance is not optional across a wide-area network, so the real trade-off during a partition is between consistency and availability.
traps: Community cloud is a NIST deployment model and multi-cloud is not; a stem listing virtual private cloud, multi-cloud and distributed cloud alongside community cloud is testing exactly that.

Broker versus carrier: the carrier carries the traffic, the broker intermediates, aggregates or arbitrages the services. Options are routinely written so both look plausible for a connectivity question.

Plausible-sounding cloud benefits such as provider-managed disaster recovery, unlimited capacity or pay-per-use pricing are not among the five essential characteristics, even though every one of them is true of real cloud offerings.

Edge questions are decided by the latency budget, not by capacity: if the wide-area round-trip time alone exceeds the control-loop deadline, no amount of scaling or extra accelerators in the region can meet it.
mnem: For the five essential characteristics, MORE-B: Measured service, On-demand self-service, Resource pooling, Elasticity (rapid), Broad network access. For the two confusable actors, the carrier carries the bits and the broker brokers the deal.

sub: Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
def: Service models describe how far up the stack the provider's responsibility reaches, running from IaaS, where the consumer manages everything above the virtualization layer, through PaaS and SaaS to serverless, where the consumer supplies only functions and configuration; deployment models describe who the infrastructure is provisioned for, namely private, community, public or hybrid.
exp:
Both taxonomies are answering a question about a boundary, and the fastest way to hold them is to draw the stack once and mark where the line falls. Take the layers as facilities and hardware, networking, storage, the hypervisor, the guest operating system, the runtime and middleware, the application, and the data. Under IaaS the provider owns everything up to and including the hypervisor and hands you a virtual machine, a volume and a virtual network; you own the guest OS, its patching, the runtime, the application and the data. Under PaaS the provider also owns the guest OS, the runtime and the middleware, and you deploy a build artefact and its configuration into a managed platform. Under SaaS the provider owns the whole stack including the application, and the consumer's remaining surface is user administration, configuration, identity integration and its own data. The consumer's control and the consumer's operational burden move together in the same direction: every layer you hand over is a layer you can no longer tune.

That gradient is what scenario questions test. A long-lived Java web application whose team wants to push its own artefact and decide how many instances run, but does not want to patch the operating system, the JVM or the web server, is a PaaS answer and not a Function-as-a-Service one, because the workload is long-lived and the team is explicitly asking to retain instance-count control. Move either of those and the answer moves: if the work is short, event-triggered and the team does not want to think about instances at all, it is FaaS; if the team insists on a specific kernel module, a custom JVM build or a particular OS patch level, it drops to IaaS.

Serverless is best defined by its execution model rather than by the word, which is a misnomer since there are obviously servers. The distinguishing properties are that the platform provisions an execution environment per unit of work, that instances scale out with concurrent demand and scale in to zero when idle, that billing is by invocation and by resource-time consumed rather than by reserved capacity, that each execution is stateless with only ephemeral local scratch space and a bounded maximum run time, and that the unit of scaling is typically one concurrent request per instance rather than many threads inside one process. The cold start follows directly from scale-to-zero: after several idle hours there is no warm environment, so the first request pays for environment creation, runtime initialisation and any code the handler runs outside the request path, which is why a function that normally answers in about 40 ms can take over two seconds on the first call. Warm invocations reuse the environment, which is also why anything expensive such as a database client or a loaded model should be initialised outside the handler so it survives across invocations. The billing unit is worth working once: a function invoked 2,000,000 times a month, running 200 ms each time with 512 MB allocated, consumes 2,000,000 x 0.2 s = 400,000 second-instances, and at 0.5 GB each that is 200,000 GB-seconds of metered compute, with nothing billed for the idle hours in between. That zero-idle property is exactly why serverless wins on spiky, low-duty-cycle workloads and loses against a steadily busy service, which is cheaper on a reserved instance. Backend-as-a-Service, meaning managed authentication, managed databases and managed storage consumed directly by a client, is the other half of what the industry calls serverless.

On deployment models, private cloud means the infrastructure is provisioned for the exclusive use of one organisation; it may be owned, managed and operated by that organisation, by a third party or a combination, and it may exist on or off premises, so on-premises is not what makes a cloud private. It is also not enough merely to have virtualized a data centre: without on-demand self-service, elasticity and measured service the result is a virtualized data centre, not a private cloud. Community cloud is provisioned for a specific community of consumers with shared concerns such as mission, security requirements, policy or compliance considerations, which is the model that describes a government cloud shared by departments, the Indian example being the GI Cloud initiative branded MeghRaj under MeitY. Hybrid cloud is a composition of two or more distinct deployment models that stay unique entities but are bound together by standardised or proprietary technology enabling data and application portability, with cloud bursting into a public cloud at peak the canonical pattern. Multi-cloud, meaning several public providers used side by side, is a procurement and architecture strategy, not a NIST deployment model.

Exam shape: the MCQ half sets one list-recall item on the four deployment models, one mapping scenario in which a described responsibility split has to be named, and very often one cold-start item, since it is the single most recognisable serverless behaviour. In the conventional half this leaf appears as compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS with examples and state which layers each party manages, which is answered best as a layered table rendered in prose, and as when would you choose serverless over a managed platform, where the marks are in the duty cycle, the cold-start tolerance and the state requirement rather than in a general preference.
facts: Under IaaS the consumer manages the guest operating system upwards; under PaaS the provider also manages the OS, runtime and middleware and the consumer deploys an artefact; under SaaS the provider manages the application itself.
Serverless functions scale to zero when idle, which is why the first request after an idle period pays a cold start for environment and runtime initialisation.
Serverless compute is metered in resource-time: 2,000,000 invocations of 200 ms at 512 MB is 400,000 second-instances, that is 200,000 GB-seconds, with no charge for idle time.
Code placed outside a function handler runs once per execution environment and is reused by warm invocations; code inside the handler runs on every invocation.
A private cloud is defined by exclusive use by a single organisation, not by being on premises; it may be off-premises and third-party operated.
Community cloud serves several organisations with shared mission, policy, security or compliance concerns; India's GI Cloud initiative, MeghRaj, under MeitY is a government example.

Hybrid cloud is a composition of two or more distinct deployment models that remain distinct entities but are bound together to allow data and application portability; cloud bursting is the classic pattern.
Multi-cloud is a strategy of using several public providers and is not one of the four NIST deployment models.
traps: PaaS versus FaaS: a long-lived application whose team wants to control how many instances run is PaaS; only when the work is short, event-driven and instance-count is not a concern does it become Function as a Service.
Hybrid versus multi-cloud: hybrid requires two or more distinct deployment models bound together, so two public providers is multi-cloud, not hybrid.
Virtualizing your own data centre does not by itself make a private cloud; without self-service provisioning, elasticity and measured service it fails the NIST characteristics test.
A slow first request after idle time is a cold start caused by scale-to-zero, not a memory-limit breach, a DNS expiry or gateway rate limiting, all of which are written in as distractors.
mnem: SPI is the standard acronym for the three service models, SaaS, PaaS, IaaS; read the letters downwards as increasing consumer control and increasing consumer responsibility, and upwards as more of the stack handed to the provider.

sub: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
def: Cloud-native architecture builds applications as disposable, externally configured, horizontally scalable services that assume the infrastructure underneath them will fail; microservices decompose the application along business capabilities into independently deployable services, a service mesh moves their cross-cutting network concerns into proxies beside them, and elasticity, high availability and load balancing are the runtime properties that make the result usable.
exp:
The premise of cloud-native design is that individual instances are cattle rather than pets: they are created from an image, they hold no state that cannot be lost, and killing one at random must be a non-event. The twelve-factor rules follow from that premise rather than being an arbitrary checklist. Configuration lives in the environment because the same artefact has to run in development and production unchanged; backing services are attached resources reached by URL because a database must be swappable without a rebuild; processes are stateless and share nothing because any request must be servable by any instance, which is what makes horizontal scaling and rolling replacement possible; disposability means fast startup and graceful shutdown on SIGTERM, because the platform will terminate instances during deploys, scale-in and node drains. Session state therefore has to move out of process memory into a shared store, and anything long-running has to be able to resume after being killed mid-flight.

Microservices partition along business capability, not along technical layer. Each service owns its own datastore, which is the hard part: once you forbid another service from reading your tables, cross-service invariants can no longer be maintained by a single database transaction, so you fall back on a saga of local transactions with compensating actions, and you accept eventual consistency between services. The benefits are independent deployability, independent scaling of hot services, fault isolation and technology freedom per service. The costs are network calls where method calls used to be, so partial failure and latency become application concerns; distributed debugging, which is what makes tracing mandatory rather than optional; schema and API versioning, since you cannot deploy every caller at once; and operational overhead per service. The anti-pattern to be able to name is the distributed monolith, in which services are split at deployment but still share a database and must be released together, so it pays every cost of distribution and collects none of the benefits.

A service mesh exists because retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, mutual TLS, load balancing and telemetry were being reimplemented in every language a team used. The mesh splits into a data plane and a control plane, and questions turn on that split. The data plane is the set of proxies deployed beside each workload, classically as a sidecar container in the same Pod; they carry every request in and out, terminate and originate mutual TLS per connection, enforce per-request retry, timeout, circuit-breaking and outlier-ejection rules, apply the traffic split for a canary, and emit per-request metrics. The control plane holds the desired configuration, exposes the operator-facing API through which routing and policy are declared, distributes that configuration to the proxies and issues and rotates their workload identity certificates. Anything happening once per request is data plane; anything about holding, reconciling or distributing configuration is control plane. Newer sidecar-less deployment modes move part of that per-request work into a per-node agent to cut the per-Pod overhead, but the plane split is unchanged.

Elasticity and high availability are separate properties and both are calculable. Elasticity means capacity tracks demand automatically in both directions and you stop paying for what you released; scalability is only the ability to grow. Horizontal scaling adds instances behind a load balancer and is the cloud-native default; vertical scaling resizes one instance and usually needs a restart. The classic failure is a control loop slower than the load it is chasing: a stateless API scaling on average CPU over a five-minute window against traffic that arrives as 30-second bursts will spike in latency and errors through each burst and only add instances after the burst has passed, then scale them back in before the next one, so the group both misses the peak and pays for capacity during the trough. Fixes are a shorter evaluation window, scaling on a leading signal such as queue depth or requests-per-instance rather than CPU, pre-warmed minimum capacity, or scheduled scaling when the pattern is predictable. High availability is arithmetic on redundancy. Components in series multiply: a request that must traverse two independent components each at 99.9% has an end-to-end availability of 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.998001, which over a 30-day month is about 86.4 minutes of downtime instead of 43.2, and a chain of five such components lands near 216 minutes. Redundant components in parallel multiply the failure probabilities instead: two independent 99.9% replicas give 1 - 0.001 x 0.001 = 0.999999, six nines, provided the failures really are independent, which is exactly what a shared availability zone, a shared power feed or a shared control plane destroys. This is why replicas are spread across availability zones, why active-active beats active-passive on recovery time, and why the number of dependencies in the request path is itself an availability decision.

Load balancing questions hinge on which layer sees what. A Layer 4 balancer forwards on IP addresses and ports, so it can distribute TCP connections, health-check backends and, because it does not terminate the connection at the application layer, preserve the client's source IP towards the backend; it cannot read a URL. A Layer 7 balancer terminates the HTTP request, so it can route by path, host, header or cookie, split traffic by weight for a canary, terminate TLS, rewrite and retry idempotent requests, and it conveys the original client address in a forwarding header because the connection to the backend is its own. Sending requests for one path prefix to one backend pool and another prefix elsewhere is therefore strictly Layer 7. Know the algorithms as a set: round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, least response time, and hashing on a key such as source IP or a cookie for affinity, with consistent hashing preferred so that adding a backend remaps only a fraction of keys. Know also active health checks, which probe endpoints, against passive checks, which eject a backend after observed failures, and connection draining, which lets in-flight requests finish while a backend is removed.

Sustainable cloud computing belongs in this same architectural conversation, because the lever that reduces carbon is the same lever that reduces waste: utilisation. An idle server draws a large fraction of its peak power while doing no work, so an estate averaging four percent utilisation is not merely expensive, it is burning most of its energy for nothing, and consolidating onto fewer, better-loaded machines is the single largest improvement available. The facility-level metric to know is power usage effectiveness, the ratio of total facility energy to the energy delivered to the IT equipment, so a perfect facility would score 1.0 and everything above that is cooling, power conversion and lighting overhead; large purpose-built data centres run close to that ideal while typical enterprise server rooms are far worse, which is a real part of why consolidation into hyperscale or shared government facilities reduces energy per unit of work. Water usage effectiveness is its counterpart for evaporative cooling, and matters in Indian climates. Carbon accounting splits into operational emissions from the electricity consumed and embodied emissions from manufacturing the hardware, and because embodied carbon is paid once at manufacture, extending hardware life and raising utilisation both amortise it better; this is why replacing a lightly loaded fleet with newer hardware is not automatically the greener choice. The architectural techniques are demand shaping and shifting: run flexible batch work when and where the grid is cleaner, since carbon intensity varies by region and by hour, place workloads in low-carbon regions when latency and data residency permit, scale to zero rather than leaving idle capacity, choose efficient instance types and accelerators for the job, and set storage lifecycle rules so cold data is not sitting on hot media. Serverless and good autoscaling are sustainability measures as well as cost measures, which is why FinOps and sustainability reporting increasingly share the same telemetry.

Exam shape: the MCQ half tends to set one data-plane-versus-control-plane item, one Layer 4 versus Layer 7 capability item and one autoscaling-behaviour scenario. In the conventional half this leaf is essay-shaped as discuss the advantages and challenges of a microservices architecture, or explain how elasticity and high availability are achieved in a cloud application, and the marks that get left behind are the quantitative ones: an answer that says redundancy improves availability without ever multiplying two numbers is worth noticeably less than one that computes the series and parallel cases.
facts: In a service mesh the sidecar proxies of the data plane carry every request, terminating and originating mutual TLS and applying retry, timeout and circuit-breaking rules; the control plane holds and distributes configuration and issues workload certificates.
Two independent components in series at 99.9% each give 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.998001, about 86.4 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month rather than 43.2.
Two independent replicas at 99.9% in parallel give 1 - 0.001 x 0.001 = 0.999999, but only if the failures are genuinely independent, which shared zones, power feeds or control planes break.
A Layer 4 load balancer forwards on IP and port and can preserve the client source IP; routing by URL path, host, header or cookie requires a Layer 7 load balancer.
Consistent hashing is preferred for session affinity because adding or removing a backend remaps only a fraction of keys rather than nearly all of them.

Each microservice owning its own datastore forces cross-service consistency to be handled by sagas of local transactions with compensating actions, giving eventual rather than transactional consistency.
A distributed monolith is a set of services that are separately deployed but share a database or must be released together, paying the costs of distribution without the benefits.
Elasticity is automatic scaling in both directions with release of unused capacity; scalability is only the ability to handle growth.
An autoscaler evaluating average CPU over a five-minute window cannot react to 30-second bursts: latency spikes during each burst and the new instances arrive after it has passed.
Power usage effectiveness is total facility energy divided by the energy delivered to the IT equipment, so 1.0 is the ideal and everything above it is cooling, power conversion and lighting overhead.

Sustainable cloud computing separates operational emissions from electricity consumed and embodied emissions from manufacturing hardware, which is why raising utilisation and extending hardware life both matter.
traps: Data plane versus control plane: anything done once per request, including mutual TLS and retries, is the sidecar's job; holding desired configuration, reconciling drift and exposing the operator API are control-plane jobs.

Layer 4 versus Layer 7: distributing TCP connections, health-checking backends and preserving the client source IP are all possible at Layer 4, so the only genuinely Layer 7 capability in a typical option set is content-based routing on path, header or cookie.
Elasticity is not the same as high availability; an autoscaling group with all instances in one availability zone is elastic and not highly available.
In series availability multiplies and gets worse with each hop, while in parallel it is the failure probabilities that multiply; using the wrong one turns a redundancy question upside down.
A lower power usage effectiveness number is better and 1.0 is the floor, so a stem offering a PUE improvement from 1.2 to 1.5 is describing a worse facility, not a greener one.
mnem: Layer 4 knows addresses and ports; Layer 7 knows paths, headers and cookies. If the question mentions a URL or a cookie, it is Layer 7.

sub: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
def: Virtualization interposes a layer that multiplexes one physical resource into several isolated virtual ones; a hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, does this for a whole machine so that each guest runs its own kernel on virtual CPU, memory, disk and network devices while the hypervisor retains control of the real hardware.
exp:
Start from the requirement rather than the product names. Popek and Goldberg set the standard for a virtual machine monitor: equivalence, meaning a program runs on the virtual machine as it would on the real one; resource control, meaning the monitor keeps complete control of the physical resources; and efficiency, meaning the great majority of instructions execute directly on the hardware rather than being interpreted. Their sufficient condition is that every sensitive instruction, one whose behaviour depends on or changes the machine's configuration, must be a privileged instruction that traps when executed outside the most privileged mode. The monitor then runs the guest kernel deprivileged and catches those traps, which is the trap-and-emulate design. Classic x86 failed this condition, because it had sensitive instructions that executed silently with different semantics in user mode instead of trapping, and that failure is the whole reason the two families of workaround exist.

Two independent axes are examined here and conflating them is the single commonest error on this leaf. The first axis is where the hypervisor sits. A Type 1, or bare-metal, hypervisor runs directly on the hardware and the guests run on it, so it schedules the physical CPUs itself; a Type 2, or hosted, hypervisor runs as a process on a general-purpose host operating system and relies on that host for scheduling and device drivers, which is why it is convenient on a workstation and slower under load. KVM is the interesting case, since it is a kernel module that turns the Linux kernel itself into the hypervisor and is normally classified as Type 1 even though a full operating system is present. The second axis is how the guest's privileged operations are handled. Full virtualization presents hardware the guest cannot distinguish from a physical machine and requires no guest modification, achieving it originally by binary translation of the offending kernel instructions and today by hardware assist, where the processor provides a separate root and non-root operating mode so guest kernel code can run at its natural privilege level and exit to the hypervisor only on defined events. Paravirtualization instead modifies the guest kernel so that sensitive operations are replaced by explicit hypercalls into the hypervisor, trading portability for lower overhead, which is the Xen lineage. The two axes are orthogonal: a Type 1 hypervisor can run fully virtualized guests, and paravirtualized device drivers such as virtio are routinely used inside an otherwise fully virtualized guest precisely because emulating a real network card is slow. Note also what paravirtualization is not: a container shares the host kernel and has no guest kernel at all, which is a different mechanism entirely.

CPU and memory virtualization is where the performance questions live. Each vCPU is a schedulable entity that the hypervisor places on a physical core, so vCPUs can be overcommitted against physical cores and the symptom of overcommitment is ready time, the interval a runnable vCPU waits for a core, which appears inside the guest as unexplained latency while guest CPU utilisation looks low. Memory needs a second translation, guest-virtual to guest-physical to host-physical; shadow page tables did this in software at high cost, and nested paging in hardware, marketed as EPT or RVI, does it in the MMU. Memory overcommitment is reclaimed by ballooning, in which a driver inside the guest allocates pages so the guest's own policy chooses what to give up, by transparent page sharing, and as a last resort by host swapping, which is the worst-performing option because the hypervisor cannot know which guest pages matter. Device assignment uses the IOMMU to give a guest direct, safely remapped access to a physical device, and SR-IOV extends that by letting one physical network card present many virtual functions that can each be assigned to a different guest, bypassing the software switch.

Storage virtualization abstracts physical capacity into pooled logical volumes. A guest disk is a file or a logical volume on a shared datastore reached over a SAN or over IP, so the guest sees a plain block device while the platform is free to move, replicate or snapshot it underneath. Thin provisioning allocates blocks on first write, so the sum of provisioned capacity may exceed physical capacity and the operational risk moves to running the pool dry; thick provisioning reserves it up front. Snapshots are copy-on-write: taking one freezes the base image and diverts new writes to a delta, which is why long-lived snapshot chains degrade write performance and are not a backup. Live migration builds on the same abstraction, iteratively pre-copying a running guest's memory to another host while it keeps running and pausing only briefly to transfer the last dirty pages.

Network virtualization is the piece with a clean calculation. Inside a host a virtual switch connects each guest's virtual NIC to the physical uplinks. Across a fabric, isolating tenants with 802.1Q VLANs alone does not scale, because the VLAN ID field is 12 bits: 2^12 = 4096 values, of which 0 and 4095 are reserved, leaving 4094 usable segments, so tens of thousands of tenants simply do not fit, and every tenant would in any case have to be trunked across the physical switches. An overlay solves both problems by encapsulating the tenant's Layer 2 frame inside an outer IP and UDP packet between the hosts, tagging it with a per-tenant network identifier in the encapsulation header. In VXLAN that identifier is 24 bits, giving 2^24 = 16,777,216 segments, and the physical fabric then only ever routes ordinary IP between host addresses, which lets tenants reuse overlapping private IPv4 ranges freely. The cost to remember is header overhead: VXLAN adds roughly 50 bytes of outer headers, so either the fabric carries jumbo frames or the guest MTU has to be reduced, and a fabric that silently fails to do either produces the classic intermittent large-packet failure.

Exam shape: the MCQ half is very reliable on this leaf, with one Type 1 versus Type 2 definition item, one full versus paravirtualization item and one applied item on multi-tenant network isolation. In the conventional half it appears as explain the types of hypervisors and compare full virtualization with paravirtualization, and as discuss CPU, storage and network virtualization techniques, where the marks come from treating the two axes separately and from naming the concrete mechanism, hypercalls, nested paging, ballooning, thin provisioning, encapsulation, rather than restating the definition.
facts: Popek and Goldberg require equivalence, resource control and efficiency of a virtual machine monitor, and require that every sensitive instruction be privileged so that it traps.
A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware; a Type 2 hypervisor runs as a process on a host operating system and depends on it for scheduling and drivers.
Full virtualization runs an unmodified guest using binary translation or hardware assist; paravirtualization modifies the guest kernel to issue explicit hypercalls to the hypervisor.
Nested paging in hardware, known as EPT or RVI, replaces software shadow page tables for the second level of guest-physical to host-physical address translation.
Ballooning reclaims guest memory by having an in-guest driver allocate pages so the guest chooses what to release; host swapping is the last-resort alternative and performs worst.
SR-IOV lets one physical NIC expose multiple virtual functions assignable directly to guests through the IOMMU, bypassing the software virtual switch.
The 802.1Q VLAN ID field is 12 bits, giving 4096 values of which 0 and 4095 are reserved, so only 4094 usable VLANs exist.
The VXLAN network identifier is 24 bits, giving 16,777,216 segments, and VXLAN encapsulation adds roughly 50 bytes, so the underlay needs a larger MTU or the guest MTU must be lowered.
Snapshots are copy-on-write deltas over a frozen base image, so long chains degrade write performance and a snapshot is not a backup.
vCPUs may be overcommitted against physical cores; the symptom is ready time, which shows up as guest latency while guest CPU utilisation appears low.
traps: Type 1 versus Type 2 is about where the hypervisor runs, bare metal against hosted on an operating system; full versus paravirtualization is about whether the guest kernel is modified to make hypercalls. Options that pair a Type-1 claim with a paravirtualization claim are exploiting exactly this confusion.
Paravirtualization does not mean the guest shares the host kernel; that description is a container. A paravirtualized guest still runs its own kernel, just a modified one.
Paravirtualized drivers such as virtio inside an otherwise fully virtualized guest are normal, so full virtualization does not imply every device is emulated.

For tens of thousands of tenants with overlapping address ranges, VLANs alone are arithmetically impossible at 4094 segments; the answer is an overlay with a per-tenant identifier in the encapsulation header, not one VLAN per tenant and not source NAT.
mnem: Type is about where the hypervisor sits; full versus para is about whether the guest knows it is a guest.
rel: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
Distributed, edge and cloud computing; NIST cloud architecture
Cloud storage, compute, networking, managed databases, monitoring and multi-cloud

sub: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
def: A container is a process on the host kernel confined by namespaces, which control what it can see, and control groups, which cap what it can consume; Docker packages such processes as layered images, Kubernetes schedules and reconciles them across a cluster, and infrastructure as code with tools such as Terraform and Ansible declares the environment they run in so it can be rebuilt identically.
exp:
A container is not a small virtual machine and every question on this leaf ultimately rests on that. There is one kernel, the host's, and the container is an ordinary process tree that has been given a restricted view of it. Namespaces provide the view: separate PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user and cgroup namespaces mean the process sees its own process numbering, its own interfaces, its own filesystem root and its own hostname. Control groups provide the accounting and the ceiling: how much CPU time, memory, block I/O and how many processes this group may consume. Isolation, then, is the pair of them, and the exam distinction is exactly that split, namespaces for visibility and cgroups for consumption. The image is a third mechanism, a stack of read-only layers assembled by a union filesystem such as overlayfs with a thin writable layer on top, which is why containers start in milliseconds and why anything written inside a container is lost when it is removed unless a volume was mounted. Because there is only one kernel, the security boundary is thinner than a hypervisor's, which is why capabilities are dropped, seccomp filters restrict syscalls, and a mandatory access control module is applied on top.

Docker's architecture is a chain worth naming: the docker client speaks over a socket to the dockerd daemon, which delegates container lifecycle to containerd, which invokes a low-level OCI runtime, runc, to create the process with the right namespaces and cgroups. The image and runtime formats are OCI standards, which is why images built with one tool run under another runtime. A Dockerfile is read as layers, one per instruction that changes the filesystem, and the build cache is invalidated at the first instruction whose inputs changed, so ordering matters: copy the dependency manifest and install dependencies before copying the application source, or every source edit rebuilds the dependency layer. Multi-stage builds compile in a fat builder stage and copy only the artefact into a minimal runtime stage, which cuts both image size and attack surface. Know that ENTRYPOINT sets the executable and CMD supplies default arguments that a run-time argument replaces, that a volume outlives the container while a bind mount exposes a host path, and that the default bridge network gives containers a private subnet with outbound NAT.

Kubernetes is a set of control loops over a declared desired state, and the components split cleanly into control plane and node. On the control plane, kube-apiserver is the only component that talks to etcd and the front door for every other component; etcd is the consistent, replicated key-value store holding all cluster state, using Raft, which is why an odd number of members is deployed and why it is the thing you back up. kube-scheduler watches for Pods with no node assigned and binds each to a node using filtering and scoring over resource requests, affinities, taints and tolerations and topology spread. kube-controller-manager runs the reconciliation loops such as the node, replicaset and endpoints controllers, and the cloud-controller-manager holds the provider-specific loops. On every node, the kubelet registers the node, receives its Pod specifications and drives the container runtime through the CRI, and reports status; kube-proxy programs the node's packet path so a Service virtual IP is distributed across its healthy endpoints. So kubelet and kube-proxy are node components and never control-plane ones. Above the Pod sit the workload objects: a Deployment manages ReplicaSets and rolls updates within maxSurge and maxUnavailable bounds, a StatefulSet gives stable identity and per-replica storage, a DaemonSet places one Pod per node, Jobs and CronJobs run to completion. Probes are separately examinable: a failing liveness probe restarts the container, while a failing readiness probe only removes it from Service endpoints, and a startup probe protects slow starters from liveness restarts.

Resource management is the highest-yield calculation on this leaf, so keep the two values distinct. The request is what the scheduler uses: it will only place a Pod on a node whose allocatable capacity minus the sum of existing requests can accommodate it, so requests, not actual usage, determine placement and bin packing. The limit is what the runtime enforces. Exceeding a CPU limit causes throttling, because CPU is compressible and the cgroup quota simply gives the process less time per period; exceeding a memory limit causes the container to be killed, because memory is incompressible and the kernel OOM killer terminates it, after which the Pod restarts and shows as OOMKilled. A container with a request of 256Mi and a limit of 512Mi is therefore scheduled against 256Mi and terminated past 512Mi, and nothing about that pair is advisory. The requests-and-limits pattern also determines the QoS class, Guaranteed when every container sets equal requests and limits for both CPU and memory, BestEffort when nothing is set, Burstable in between, and that class is the eviction order under node pressure, BestEffort first. Setting requests too high wastes capacity across the cluster; setting them too low means Pods are scheduled onto nodes that cannot really carry them.

Infrastructure as code splits into provisioning and configuration and the syllabus names one tool for each, so do not blur them. Terraform is declarative provisioning: you write the desired infrastructure in HCL, a provider plugin translates it to cloud API calls, and a state file records the mapping between your declared resources and the real ones, which is what lets a plan show the diff before an apply and what makes drift and destroy possible at all. State is therefore the thing that must be stored remotely and locked when a team shares it. Ansible is primarily agentless configuration management: it pushes over SSH, or WinRM for Windows, executes modules on the target and removes them, so nothing has to be installed on managed nodes beyond a Python interpreter and SSH access. Its playbooks are YAML task lists that are ordered and procedural in execution while individual modules are written to be idempotent, and it keeps no state file, deriving current state by inspecting the host each run. The common summary is that Terraform builds the servers and Ansible configures what runs inside them; the exam version of that sentence is routinely offered with the two swapped. Alongside this sits the immutable-infrastructure idea, in which you never patch a running instance but bake a new image and replace it, which is why containers and IaC reinforce each other.

CI/CD and DevOps practice close the leaf. Continuous integration means every change merges to the mainline frequently with an automated build and test gate; continuous delivery means every build that passes is releasable and the release is a decision; continuous deployment means it ships automatically. The discipline that matters is build once and promote the same artefact through environments, with environment differences injected as configuration, since rebuilding per environment means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped. Release strategies are worth distinguishing: rolling replaces instances gradually, blue-green stands up a full parallel environment and switches traffic with instant rollback at double the cost, and canary sends a small traffic share to the new version and promotes on observed metrics. GitOps applies the same reconciliation idea to delivery, keeping the desired cluster state in Git and letting an in-cluster agent pull and converge it. The commonly cited DevOps outcome metrics are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service.

Exam shape: expect one requests-versus-limits item, one Terraform-versus-Ansible item and one containers-fundamentals item in the MCQ half, plus component attribution questions that simply ask which process does what. In the conventional half this leaf is essay-shaped as explain the architecture of Kubernetes with its control-plane and node components, and as what is infrastructure as code and how do CI/CD pipelines support DevOps practices. Marks are lost by describing Kubernetes as though it were a scheduler alone, when the examinable idea is a declared desired state continuously reconciled by controllers.
facts: Namespaces control what a container can see, PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC and user; control groups cap what it can consume, CPU time, memory, block I/O and process count.
The Docker chain runs docker client to dockerd to containerd to runc, with image and runtime formats standardised by the OCI.
kube-apiserver is the only component that talks to etcd; etcd is the replicated Raft-based key-value store holding all cluster state.
kube-scheduler binds unscheduled Pods to nodes and kube-controller-manager runs the reconciliation loops; kubelet and kube-proxy run on every node and are not control-plane components.
Resource requests drive scheduling and bin packing; limits are enforced at runtime, with CPU throttled beyond its limit and memory causing an OOM kill beyond its limit.

QoS class is Guaranteed when requests equal limits for CPU and memory in every container, BestEffort when neither is set, and Burstable otherwise; BestEffort Pods are evicted first under node pressure.
A failing liveness probe restarts the container; a failing readiness probe only removes the Pod from Service endpoints.

Terraform is declarative provisioning that reconciles a configuration against a recorded state file to create, change or destroy resources; that state file is what makes plan, drift detection and destroy possible.
Ansible is primarily agentless configuration management, pushing over SSH or WinRM, keeping no state file and determining current state by inspecting the host each run.
Blue-green deployment keeps a full parallel environment and switches traffic for instant rollback; canary shifts a small share of traffic to the new version and promotes on observed metrics.
traps: Requests versus limits: the request is what the scheduler places against, the limit is what the runtime enforces. Exceeding a CPU limit throttles, exceeding a memory limit kills. Options that swap throttling and termination between the two resources are the standard distractor.

Terraform versus Ansible: Terraform provisions infrastructure and keeps state, Ansible configures existing hosts agentlessly and keeps none. Options reversing this, or calling Terraform imperative and Ansible stateful, are written to look symmetrical.

kubelet and kube-proxy are node components; a question asking which component the control plane comprises is testing whether you place them correctly, and etcd is only ever reached through the API server.
Namespaces versus cgroups: a question asking what caps CPU and memory is asking for cgroups, while namespaces answer what a container can see. Union filesystem layers and seccomp filters are neither.
Liveness and readiness probes are not interchangeable; using a liveness probe where a readiness probe is meant turns a temporary dependency outage into a restart loop.
mnem: Requests get you in the door, limits get you thrown out: on CPU you are throttled, on memory you are killed.
rel: Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization
Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
Cloud security and governance: shared responsibility, IAM, Zero Trust, DevSecOps, FinOps and SLAs

sub: Cloud storage, compute, networking, managed databases, monitoring and multi-cloud
def: This leaf covers the building blocks a cloud platform actually sells: object, block and file storage; virtual and serverless compute; software-defined networking in a virtual private cloud; managed database services; the metrics, logs and traces that make the result observable; OpenStack as the open-source private-cloud implementation of all of it; and the management of hybrid, multi-cloud and AI/ML infrastructure on top.
exp:
Storage first, because the choice between the three shapes is decided by the access pattern and nothing else. Object storage exposes a flat namespace of whole objects with rich metadata over an HTTP API; an update replaces the entire object rather than editing bytes in place, durability comes from erasure coding or replication spread across zones, and lifecycle rules move cold objects to cheaper tiers. That makes it right for backups, media archives, static web assets and data lakes, and wrong for anything doing small random in-place writes. Block storage presents a raw device the guest formats and mounts, gives low and predictable latency for small random I/O, and is normally attached to one instance, which is why the data files of a transactional relational database belong on block storage and never on object storage. File storage offers a shared POSIX namespace over NFS or SMB, which is what legacy applications and shared home directories need. Two numeric ideas are examinable here. Durability and availability are different promises: durability is the probability the bytes still exist, availability the probability you can reach them right now, and a cold archive tier can be extremely durable while being deliberately slow to retrieve. And the redundancy arithmetic differs: three-way replication costs 200 percent storage overhead to tolerate two losses, while an erasure code splitting an object into six data and three parity fragments stores nine fragments for six, a 1.5 times overhead, and still tolerates the loss of any three.

Compute is the same abstraction sold at several commitment levels. Instance families are cut by resource ratio, general purpose, compute optimised, memory optimised, storage optimised and accelerated, and the purchasing axis is orthogonal: on-demand for unpredictable work, a committed or reserved term for steady baseline load in exchange for a substantial discount, and spot or preemptible capacity, which is far cheaper but may be reclaimed with short notice and therefore suits fault-tolerant, checkpointed batch work only. Above that sit autoscaling groups and, at the far end, serverless compute where no instance is bought at all. The design instinct to carry is that baseline goes on committed capacity, spiky and interruptible work goes on spot, and only the unpredictable remainder pays on-demand rates.

Cloud networking is a software-defined virtual private cloud with an address range you choose, divided into subnets pinned to availability zones. A subnet is public or private according to its route table: a route to an internet gateway makes it public, while private subnets reach outward through a NAT gateway that permits egress without allowing inbound connections. Two filtering mechanisms exist and their difference is a favourite item: security groups attach to instance interfaces, allow rules only and are stateful, so return traffic for an allowed flow is automatically permitted, whereas network ACLs attach to subnets, support allow and deny, are stateless and therefore need explicit rules in both directions. Peering between virtual networks is not transitive, which is why hub-and-spoke transit constructs exist; private endpoints keep traffic to managed services off the public internet; and connectivity to on-premises runs over IPsec VPN or a dedicated private circuit. Remember that inter-zone and outbound data transfer is billed, so chatty cross-zone architectures are a cost defect as well as a latency defect.

Managed databases sell the operational work: provisioning, patching, backup and point-in-time recovery, failover and monitoring, while you retain schema, queries and indexing. Two replication constructs are constantly confused. A synchronous standby in a second availability zone exists for high availability, is not readable, and is promoted on failure; an asynchronous read replica exists to scale reads, is readable, and lags, so a read issued immediately after a write may not see it. Choosing a replica for high availability, or a standby for read scaling, is the classic wrong answer. Beyond relational engines the families to name are key-value, document, wide-column and graph, chosen by access pattern, with the general trade that a NoSQL store buys horizontal partitioning and flexible schema by giving up cross-partition joins and, often, strict cross-row transactions. Practical cloud specifics worth holding are that connection-heavy applications need a pooler or proxy because each connection costs server memory, that a read-heavy workload usually wants a cache in front rather than a bigger instance, and that analytical queries belong in a columnar warehouse rather than on the transactional primary.

Monitoring tells you whether a known thing is broken; observability is the property that you can ask new questions of a system from its telemetry without shipping new code. The signals are metrics, numeric time series that are cheap to store and aggregate but lose per-request detail; logs, discrete events that are rich but expensive at volume; and distributed traces, which record one request's path across services. Tracing is the one that answers the multi-service latency question. Each request gets a trace identifier and each hop emits a span with a parent, and the context is propagated in request headers across every service, so a single trace shows exactly which of eight hops consumed the time, something no per-service latency dashboard can reveal because each service's own share may look entirely normal. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral instrumentation and wire standard for all three signals, which is what keeps this portable across providers. Sampling controls cost, head-based deciding at the start and tail-based deciding after the trace completes so that slow and failed requests can be kept preferentially. Alerting practice is to alert on user-visible symptoms and error-budget burn against a stated service level objective rather than on causes, and to read latency at high percentiles rather than as a mean, since an average hides precisely the tail that users experience. Watch label cardinality: a metric labelled with a user or request identifier multiplies into millions of series.

OpenStack is the open-source IaaS platform that implements all of the above on your own hardware, and it matters for Indian government and academic private clouds. Its core projects are worth naming individually: Nova for compute, Neutron for networking, Cinder for block storage, Swift for object storage, Glance for the image service, Keystone for identity and the service catalogue, and Horizon for the dashboard, with Heat providing template-driven orchestration and Ironic provisioning bare metal. Every service exposes a REST API and they authenticate against Keystone, which is the piece to remember because it is the single point every other component depends on.

Hybrid and multi-cloud management is where this leaf turns from components into governance. The motives are regulatory or data-residency constraints, avoiding concentration and lock-in, keeping a legacy estate, and using a genuinely better service from another provider. The costs are real: duplicated expertise and tooling, egress charges when data crosses providers, and the pressure to design for the lowest common denominator. It is worth being precise about what actually blocks portability, because the intuitive answers are wrong. Container images are an OCI standard and run anywhere; kernel versions and TCP/IP are not the problem. What binds you is provider-specific managed services, the identity and permission model, the managed database, the queue, the object-storage API and the event plumbing, none of which have a common interface to target. The mitigations are correspondingly specific: use Kubernetes as the common runtime substrate, one infrastructure-as-code tool across providers, federated identity rather than parallel user directories, centralised observability and cost reporting, and a deliberate decision about which managed services you are willing to be locked into. AI and ML infrastructure is the newest member of this list and stresses the same primitives differently: accelerator instances with high-bandwidth interconnect for distributed training, high-throughput parallel storage for the training set, and a serving tier whose scaling problem is that model weights take a long time to load, so scaling to zero is often unaffordable. Data gravity dominates the placement decision, because moving a multi-terabyte training set between regions or providers costs more in time and egress than the compute saved, and around all of it sits MLOps: feature stores, a model registry, reproducible pipelines and drift monitoring in production.

Exam shape: the MCQ half samples this leaf as storage-type fit, an observability item that is almost always about tracing, and a portability or cost item. In the conventional half it appears as compare object, block and file storage with suitable use cases, as explain the OpenStack architecture and its major components, and as discuss the challenges of hybrid and multi-cloud management. Marks are lost by listing components without saying which access pattern or which failure each one answers.
facts: Object storage replaces whole objects rather than updating bytes in place, so a transactional database doing small random in-place writes belongs on block storage.
Durability is the probability the data still exists; availability is the probability it can be retrieved now, and an archive tier can be highly durable yet slow to access.

Three-way replication is a 200 percent storage overhead to tolerate two losses; a six-data-plus-three-parity erasure code stores nine fragments for six, a 1.5 times overhead, and tolerates any three losses.
Spot or preemptible capacity is the cheapest compute but can be reclaimed at short notice, so it suits only fault-tolerant, checkpointed batch work.
Security groups are stateful, attach to instance interfaces and hold allow rules only; network ACLs are stateless, attach to subnets and support both allow and deny, needing rules in both directions.
A subnet is public or private by its route table: a route to an internet gateway makes it public, while a NAT gateway gives private subnets outbound access without inbound reachability.
A synchronous standby in another availability zone provides high availability and is not readable; an asynchronous read replica scales reads and lags behind the primary.
The three telemetry signals are metrics, logs and traces; distributed tracing propagates a trace context across every hop so each span's duration is attributable within one request.
OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for instrumenting and exporting metrics, logs and traces.
OpenStack core projects are Nova for compute, Neutron for networking, Cinder for block storage, Swift for object storage, Glance for images, Keystone for identity and Horizon for the dashboard.
Multi-cloud portability is limited in practice by provider-specific managed services and identity models, not by container image formats, kernel versions or networking protocols.
traps: Object storage is not a drop-in for a database volume; the give-away in a stem is small random in-place updates, which object storage cannot do because a write replaces the whole object.

Read replica versus multi-AZ standby: the replica is asynchronous and readable and scales reads, the standby is synchronous and not readable and exists for failover. Each is offered as the answer to the other's question.
Security group versus network ACL: because security groups are stateful, adding an outbound rule for return traffic is unnecessary there but mandatory on a stateless network ACL.
Blaming multi-cloud portability failures on incompatible image formats or kernel differences is the plausible wrong answer; the real coupling is to managed services and IAM.
When every individual service dashboard looks healthy but the end-to-end request is slow, more logs or finer host metrics will not localise it; only a trace that spans the whole request will.
mnem: OpenStack core: Nova computes, Neutron networks, Cinder gives blocks, Swift holds objects, Glance keeps images, Keystone keys the door, Horizon is the view.
rel: Cloud-native architecture, microservices, service mesh, elasticity and load balancing
Deployment and service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
