Virtualization: virtual machines, hypervisors, and CPU/storage/network virtualization

sub: Cloud security and governance: shared responsibility, IAM, Zero Trust, DevSecOps, FinOps and SLAs
def: Cloud security and governance is the division of security duties between provider and customer under the shared responsibility model, the identity, authentication and Zero Trust controls the customer must operate on its own side of that line, the protective measures of encryption, backup, disaster recovery, container and API hardening and DevSecOps, and the commercial governance exercised through FinOps and service level agreements.
exp:
The shared responsibility model is the organising idea and everything else in the leaf hangs off it. The provider is responsible for the security of the cloud, meaning the physical facilities and their access control, the host hardware, the storage fabric, the network backbone and the hypervisor and managed-service software it operates. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud, and where that line falls moves with the service model. On IaaS the customer owns the guest operating system and its patching, the runtime, the application, the network and firewall configuration and the data. On PaaS the platform takes the operating system and runtime, leaving the customer the application code, its configuration, identity and data. On SaaS the customer's remaining surface is user and access administration, tenant configuration and the data itself. What never transfers, at any service model, is responsibility for your own data, for who is allowed to touch it, and for the access configuration that decides it. That is why the overwhelming majority of real cloud incidents are customer-side misconfiguration, a storage container left publicly readable or a role granted far more than it needs, rather than a compromise of the provider's own infrastructure.

Identity and access management is the primary control plane of a cloud estate, because in a software-defined environment an over-permissive credential is equivalent to physical access. The model is principals, which are human users, groups, roles and workload or service identities; policies, which grant or deny named actions on named resources, optionally under conditions; and an evaluation rule that is default deny, with an explicit deny always overriding any allow. Effective permission is therefore the intersection of everything applicable, narrowed further by organisation-level guardrails and permission boundaries, which cap what any policy inside a scope can grant even if an administrator writes a wider one. The practices that follow are least privilege granted per resource and per action rather than by wildcard; roles assumed for short-lived, automatically rotated credentials in preference to long-lived static access keys, which are the single most commonly leaked cloud secret; workload identity for applications so that no key is embedded in code or an image at all; federation of human identity from the corporate directory over SAML or OIDC so that joiners and leavers are handled once; separation of duties and just-in-time elevation for privileged actions; and secrets held in a managed vault rather than in configuration files or environment values checked into a repository. Know the difference between role-based access control, which grants by assigned role, and attribute-based access control, which decides from attributes of the subject, resource, action and context and therefore scales better across a large, tag-organised estate. In Indian public-sector practice this sits inside a wider compliance frame: the CERT-In directions require reporting of specified cyber incidents within six hours of noticing them and retention of ICT logs within Indian jurisdiction for 180 days, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act places obligations on the data fiduciary that do not move to the cloud provider simply because the workload did.

Multi-factor authentication addresses the fact that a password alone is a single, phishable, reusable secret. A factor is something you know, something you have or something you are, and genuine multi-factor authentication requires factors from different categories, which is why a password plus a security question is still single-factor. The factor types are not equal in strength. SMS one-time passcodes are the weakest common option because they are interceptable and vulnerable to SIM swap; time-based one-time passcodes from an authenticator application are stronger but still phishable in real time by a proxy site that relays the code; push approvals are vulnerable to fatigue attacks, where an attacker repeatedly prompts a user until one is approved, which number matching mitigates. Phishing-resistant authentication using FIDO2 and WebAuthn hardware-backed credentials is the current standard, because the credential is cryptographically bound to the origin and cannot be replayed against a look-alike site. The operational rules to remember are that the root or break-glass account must have hardware multi-factor authentication and be used almost never, that privileged and administrative API actions should require it, and that recovery paths must not quietly bypass it.

Zero Trust is the architecture that follows from admitting the network perimeter no longer marks a trust boundary. Its premise is never trust, always verify: no request is trusted because of where it came from, every access decision is made per session against the identity of the requester, the posture and compliance of the device, the sensitivity of the resource and contextual signals, and all traffic is encrypted and authenticated including traffic that stays inside the data centre. Structurally, the decision is made by a policy engine, applied by a policy administrator, and imposed at a policy enforcement point sitting in front of every resource, so access is mediated at the resource rather than at the network edge. Assume-breach is the design stance, which is why micro-segmentation matters: an attacker who compromises one workload should find no implicit lateral path to the next. Contrast this with the castle-and-moat model, where a virtual private network admits a device to a flat internal network and everything inside is implicitly trusted, which is precisely how a single stolen laptop becomes a domain-wide incident. In a cloud estate the concrete pieces are workload identity, mutual TLS between services enforced by a service mesh, network policies that default to deny, an identity-aware proxy in front of internal applications and conditional access based on device compliance. Zero Trust is an architecture and a set of tenets, not a product you can buy.

Encryption is layered by state. At rest, server-side encryption normally uses envelope encryption: the data is encrypted with a data encryption key, and that key is itself encrypted by a key encryption key held in a managed key service or hardware security module, so rotating the master key does not require rewriting the data. Keys may be provider-managed, customer-managed, which gives you the ability to audit use and to revoke, or customer-supplied. In transit, TLS protects north-south traffic and mutual TLS authenticates both ends of east-west service traffic. In use, confidential computing encrypts memory and runs the workload in a hardware-protected enclave so that even a privileged host administrator cannot read it. The misconception to kill early is that encryption is not access control: a storage bucket that is encrypted at rest and also world-readable is fully readable by the world, because the service transparently decrypts for any principal it authorises.

Backup and disaster recovery are examined through two objectives that must never be swapped. The recovery point objective is the maximum tolerable data loss, measured backwards from the incident to the last usable copy; the recovery time objective is the maximum tolerable time to restore service, measured forwards. Work an example: if backups run nightly at midnight and the failure occurs at 16:00, sixteen hours of data are gone, so a stated recovery point objective of four hours cannot be met by that schedule no matter how quickly you restore, and meeting it requires more frequent backups or continuous replication. Independently, if the restore itself takes four hours, the recovery time objective is four hours even if the recovery point objective were zero. The strategies form a cost ladder: backup and restore, cheapest with recovery in hours or days; pilot light, with core data replicated and minimal services running; warm standby, a scaled-down but live copy; and multi-site active-active, with near-zero objectives at close to double the cost. Hold the 3-2-1 rule, three copies on two media types with one off-site, extended for ransomware by keeping at least one copy immutable or offline, since an attacker with the same credentials as your backup job will delete the backups first. Finally, an untested backup is not a backup: restore testing, not backup success, is the evidence, and a disaster recovery plan that has never been rehearsed will have its recovery time objective discovered during the disaster.

Container and Kubernetes security follows from the single shared kernel. Because the boundary is thinner than a hypervisor's, hardening runs across the whole lifecycle: minimal base images and multi-stage builds to shrink the attack surface, vulnerability scanning and a software bill of materials for every image, signed images with admission control that refuses unsigned ones, no secrets baked into layers, and at run time a non-root user, a read-only root filesystem, dropped Linux capabilities and a seccomp profile. In the cluster, Kubernetes role-based access control must be least-privilege rather than cluster-admin for convenience, service account tokens should not be automounted where they are not used, secrets must be encrypted at rest in etcd and preferably sourced from an external vault, network policies should default to deny so that Pods cannot reach arbitrary Pods, and admission policy should be enforced as code. Access to the API server and to etcd is the crown-jewel path, since etcd holds every secret in the cluster. For genuinely hostile multi-tenancy the shared kernel is not enough and a sandboxed runtime or one cluster per tenant is the answer.

DevSecOps is the practice of moving those controls into the pipeline rather than into a pre-release audit, on the reasoning that the cost of a defect rises sharply with the distance between introduction and discovery. A mature pipeline runs static application security testing on source, software composition analysis on dependencies, secret scanning on commits, infrastructure-as-code scanning on Terraform and Kubernetes manifests before they are applied, image scanning at build, and dynamic testing against a deployed environment, with defined gates that fail the build rather than emitting an advisory nobody reads. Around it sits supply-chain assurance, signed artefacts and recorded build provenance, and policy as code so that a rule is enforced identically in the pipeline and at admission. The cultural half is that security is a shared responsibility of the delivery team with security engineers embedded as enablers, not a gate at the end.

API security is where cloud applications are actually attacked, and the dominant class is authorisation rather than injection. Broken object-level authorisation, in which an endpoint checks that you are logged in but not that the object identifier you passed belongs to you, is the archetype and is only fixable by an ownership check on the server for every object accessed; obscure identifiers are not a control. The rest of the list is broken authentication, excessive data exposure where an endpoint returns a full record and expects the client to hide fields, missing rate limiting and quota, broken function-level authorisation where an administrative route is reachable simply by knowing it, and server-side request forgery, which is especially dangerous in cloud because it can be pointed at the instance metadata service to steal role credentials. Practical controls are OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens and full validation of signature, issuer, audience and expiry, mutual TLS between services, a gateway enforcing schema validation, rate limits and quotas, and never relying on a check performed only in the client.

Virtualization attacks are the multi-tenancy-specific threats. VM escape is the breach of the guest-to-hypervisor boundary and is the most serious because it defeats tenant isolation; hyperjacking is the insertion of a malicious hypervisor beneath a running operating system; cross-VM side channels infer secrets from shared cache and other microarchitectural state, the speculative-execution class being the well-known example, mitigated by microcode, scheduling co-tenants carefully and disabling opportunistic page sharing; snapshot and image theft is often easier than any of these, since a snapshot contains memory and credentials; and VM sprawl leaves unpatched, forgotten instances as entry points. Mitigations are prompt hypervisor patching, dedicated hosts or confidential computing for sensitive workloads, encrypted images and snapshots, and remembering that inter-VM traffic inside a host never crosses a physical network tap, so monitoring must be virtual.

FinOps is governance of variable spend, and its shape is a cycle of inform, optimise and operate. Inform means allocation: consistent tagging, showback or chargeback to the team that caused the spend, and unit economics such as cost per transaction or per customer rather than a single total. Optimise means the levers, in the order that matters: first eliminate waste, that is idle and orphaned resources, unattached volumes, forgotten environments and oversized instances, then rightsize and schedule non-production capacity off outside working hours, then apply storage lifecycle policies, then move interruptible work to spot capacity, and only then buy committed-use or reserved capacity for the baseline that remains. The ordering is the examinable point. Faced with 200 always-on virtual machines averaging four percent CPU, the FinOps action is to rightsize and consolidate, because purchasing a one-year commitment at the current sizes locks in the waste for a year, and moving to a larger family only makes the utilisation percentage look worse. Operate means making it continuous, with anomaly alerting, budgets and the engineering team owning its own cost as it owns its own reliability.

Service level agreements close the governance loop. Distinguish the service level indicator, the actual measurement such as the proportion of successful requests; the service level objective, the internal target for that indicator; and the service level agreement, the contractual commitment with a remedy attached. The arithmetic must be at your fingertips, computed over a 30-day month of 43,200 minutes: 99 percent permits 432 minutes, that is 7 hours 12 minutes; 99.9 percent permits 43.2 minutes; 99.95 percent permits 21.6 minutes; 99.99 percent permits 4.32 minutes, about 4 minutes 19 seconds; and 99.999 percent permits 0.432 minutes, about 26 seconds. Over a 365-day year the same figures are 3.65 days, 8.76 hours, 52.6 minutes and 5.26 minutes respectively. Read the fine print as carefully as the number: what counts as downtime and how it is measured, the measurement window, the exclusions for scheduled maintenance, force majeure, beta services and customer misconfiguration, and the fact that the remedy is almost always a service credit against a future bill, capped at a fraction of the monthly charge, which does not compensate business loss. Remember also that composing dependent services multiplies their availabilities, so a chain of components each at 99.9 percent delivers less than 99.9 percent end to end, and no provider commitment can be inherited by your own service without that computation.

Exam shape: the MCQ half of this leaf is dense with one-mark items, a shared-responsibility attribution, an RPO or RTO definition, an availability-to-downtime conversion and a FinOps action question. The conventional half draws more essay questions from here than from anywhere else in the unit, because explain the shared responsibility model across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, discuss Zero Trust security architecture and its principles, describe a disaster recovery strategy with RPO and RTO for a government application, explain DevSecOps and the security controls in a CI/CD pipeline, and enumerate the clauses that a cloud SLA should contain are all natural ten-mark prompts. In every one of those, marks come from concreteness: name the control, state on which side of the line it falls, and where the topic is numeric, do the arithmetic.
facts: Under shared responsibility the provider secures the cloud, meaning facilities, hardware, network and hypervisor, and the customer secures what is in it; the customer's data, identity management and access configuration never transfer at any service model.
In cloud IAM the evaluation is default deny and an explicit deny always overrides an allow; organisation guardrails and permission boundaries cap what any policy inside their scope can grant.
Assumed roles issue short-lived automatically rotated credentials, which is why they are preferred over long-lived static access keys.

Genuine multi-factor authentication needs factors from different categories, so a password plus a security question is still single-factor; FIDO2 and WebAuthn are phishing-resistant because the credential is bound to the origin, while SMS and time-based codes are not.

Zero Trust makes a per-session access decision using identity, device posture and context at a policy enforcement point in front of each resource, decided by a policy engine and applied by a policy administrator, and it assumes breach rather than trusting network location.

Envelope encryption encrypts data with a data encryption key that is itself wrapped by a key encryption key in a managed key service, so rotating the master key does not require re-encrypting the data.
RPO is the maximum tolerable data loss measured back to the last usable copy; RTO is the maximum tolerable time to restore service.
The 3-2-1 rule is three copies on two media types with one off-site, extended against ransomware by keeping at least one copy immutable or offline.

Broken object-level authorisation, where an endpoint verifies authentication but not ownership of the requested object, is the archetypal API vulnerability; server-side request forgery is especially dangerous in cloud because it can target the instance metadata service.

VM escape breaches the guest-to-hypervisor boundary; hyperjacking installs a malicious hypervisor beneath the operating system; cross-VM side channels infer secrets from shared microarchitectural state.
The FinOps cycle is inform, optimise and operate, and the optimisation order is eliminate waste and rightsize first, commit to reserved capacity only for the baseline that remains.
Over a 30-day month of 43,200 minutes, 99 percent permits 432 minutes of downtime, 99.9 percent permits 43.2 minutes, 99.99 percent permits 4.32 minutes and 99.999 percent permits about 26 seconds.
An SLA's usual remedy is a service credit against a future bill, capped and excluding scheduled maintenance, force majeure and customer misconfiguration, so it does not compensate business loss.
traps: RPO versus RTO: the recovery point is how much data you can afford to lose looking backwards, the recovery time is how long you can afford to be down looking forwards. Stems supply both a backup interval and a restore duration to see whether you attach each to the right objective.

The shared responsibility line moves with the service model, so patching the guest OS is the customer's job on IaaS but not on PaaS; patching the hypervisor, physical access control and replacing failed disks are always the provider's.
Encryption at rest is not access control: an encrypted storage bucket that is publicly readable is still fully readable, because the service decrypts transparently for any principal it authorises.

The FinOps answer to a badly under-utilised always-on fleet is to rightsize and consolidate first; buying a reserved or committed term at the current oversized shape locks the waste in, and moving to a larger family only lowers the utilisation figure further.
Type of factor matters in MFA: two things you know are not two factors, and an SMS or app-generated code is phishable in real time whereas an origin-bound hardware credential is not.

A provider's headline availability figure is per service; chaining several dependent services multiplies their availabilities, so your end-to-end number is always lower than any single component's commitment.
mnem: RPO looks backwards to the last good copy, so it is how much data you lose; RTO looks forwards to service restored, so it is how long you are down. For downtime, start from 99.9 percent equals 43.2 minutes a month and move the decimal one place for each extra nine.
